column2: If a king's minister or his own son governs unrighteously, appointed to the seat of dharma, bull among men,
king's followers appointed to affairs who do not act rightly, putting themselves first, the lords of the earth (are to be restrained) together with those below,
the lord of the earth is ever the lord of the lordless, of men oppressed by the strong who cry out piteously and much.
Then the force of witnesses in a doubtful case is good, where the dispute has been made; the case without witnesses or without a protector is especially to be examined.
He should apply punishment to sinners corresponding to the offence; he should trouble the rich by wealth and the poor by killing and binding.
A king should protect the good by conciliation and gifts, and ill-behaved people by discipline and even blows.
One who wishes to slay a king should meet a strange death, and so should a livelihood-cheat, a thief and one who mixes classes.
For a lord of the earth rightly applying the rod, lord of men, or an appointed official, there is no unrighteousness; here dharma alone is eternal.
One who applies the rod at will, unskilled, becomes joined to infamy here and after death gets hell.
He should not impose punishment on others merely on hearsay; having examined sources and tradition, he should bind or release.
A king should never kill an envoy in any calamity; the slayer of an envoy goes to hell with his ministers.
If a king devoted to kshatriya dharma slays an envoy who speaks as instructed, his ancestors incur the sin of slaying an embryo.
An envoy should have seven qualities: well born, of good conduct, eloquent, skilled, pleasant-spoken, speaking as told, and mindful.
Endowed with these same qualities should be his doorkeeper and protector; and the chief guard should be endowed with these qualities.
One who knows the truth of the sciences of dharma and wealth should be the officer of peace and war: intelligent, steadfast, wise, and a keeper of secrets.
A praised minister is well born, endowed with truth and capable; endowed with these same qualities the general should be.
He should know the truth of arrays, machines and weapons, be valiant, able to bear rain, cold, heat and wind, and know the weak points of others.
He should inspire trust in others but trust no one; even in sons, O king, trust is not praised.
This is the essence of the scripture's meaning, told to you by me, blameless one: distrust is called the supreme secret of kings."

Where one is to dwell with sons, brothers and kin, Kaunteya, it is right to inquire about protection and livelihood, Bharata.
mahabharata:12:87.3	Therefore I will tell you especially about the work of forts; hearing it, it should be done and carried out with effort.
mahabharata:12:87.4	Relying on a sixfold fort, he should settle cities, where all wealth is chief or abundance would be.
mahabharata:12:87.5	The desert fort, the earth fort, the mountain fort, the human fort, the water fort and the forest fort—these are the six.
mahabharata:12:87.6	A city furnished with fort, supplied with grain and weapons, with strong ramparts and moat, crowded with elephants, horses and chariots,
mahabharata:12:87.7	where there are learned men and artisans and well-stored stocks, where the people are righteous and have attained the highest skill,
mahabharata:12:87.8	crowded with great men, elephants and horses, adorned with crossroads and shops, of established dealings, peaceful and free from fear,
mahabharata:12:87.9	of fair radiance and echoing sound, with a well-praised layout, filled with brave and wealthy people, resounding with Vedic recitation.
mahabharata:12:87.11	There he should increase treasury, army, friends and trade; in the city and the country he should remove all faults.
mahabharata:12:87.12	He should carefully increase the arsenals and treasuries and increase all stores, and also machines and maces.
mahabharata:12:87.13	Wood, iron, chaff, charcoal, timber, horn, bone and bamboo, marrow, oil, fat, honey and herbs,
mahabharata:12:87.14	hemp, resin, grain, weapons and arrows, hides, sinews, cane, munja and balbaja grass, and bows.
mahabharata:12:87.15	Reservoirs and wells with abundant water, and milk-giving trees, should always be preserved by the king.
mahabharata:12:87.16	Teachers, priests, household priests, great archers, architects, astrologers and physicians should be honoured with effort,
mahabharata:12:87.17	wise, intelligent, self-controlled, skilled, brave, learned, well born, strong in sattva, and engaged in all works.
mahabharata:12:87.18	The king should honour the righteous, restrain the unrighteous, and with effort set all classes to their own works.
mahabharata:12:87.19	Having thoroughly learned through spies the outer and inner people of town and country, he should then assign work.
mahabharata:12:87.20	Spies, counsel, treasury, and especially counsel, the king himself should attend to, for everything here is based on these.
mahabharata:12:87.21	All that the neutral, the enemy and friends intend should be known in city and country with the eye of spies.
mahabharata:12:87.22	Then all should be arranged without carelessness, ever honouring the devoted and restraining the hostile.
mahabharata:12:87.23	One should always sacrifice with sacrifices and give without oppression; protection of subjects should be done, and no censured deed.
mahabharata:12:87.24	He should always provide security, welfare and livelihood for the wretched, helpless, aged, widows and women.
mahabharata:12:87.25	In the hermitages, in due time, a king should always send clothing, vessels and food, honouring and not disregarding.
mahabharata:12:87.26	He should entrust himself, all affairs and the kingdom to an ascetic, and always remain humble with effort.
mahabharata:12:87.27	A king should honour with bed, seat and food a man renouncing all aims, well born and learned, on seeing such a one.
mahabharata:12:87.28	In him a king should place trust in any calamity, though robbers also place trust in ascetics.
mahabharata:12:87.29	In him he should deposit treasures and take counsel, but not attend him constantly or honour him too much.
mahabharata:12:87.30	Another such should be made in one's own kingdom, another in other kingdoms, another in forests and in the cities of neighbours.
mahabharata:12:87.31	To them he should give honours, refinements and shares, as in his own country, for those stationed in other kingdoms and forests.
mahabharata:12:87.32	Those ascetics of keen vows, in any condition, would give refuge to a king seeking refuge, as they wish.
mahabharata:12:87.33	This summary of the marks has been told to you briefly, of the kind of city a king should himself dwell in.

Protection of the kingdom and collection of the kingdom I shall tell you rightly; hear it all, in truth, with a single mind.
mahabharata:12:88.3	A lord of a village should be appointed, then a lord of ten villages, and likewise of twenty, a hundred and a thousand.
mahabharata:12:88.4	The village headman should look after the village's affairs and faults; he should report to the lord of ten, who reports to the lord of twenty.
mahabharata:12:88.5	He too, the lord of twenty, should report all conduct in the countryside to the guardian of a hundred villages.
mahabharata:12:88.6	Whatever is enjoyed by the villagers, the headman may enjoy; he should be supported by the lord of ten, and he by the lord of twice that.
mahabharata:12:88.7	The overseer of a hundred villages deserves to enjoy a village, honoured, a great, prosperous one crowded with people, Bharata; in it much depends on the king.
mahabharata:12:88.8	The lord of a thousand deserves the best branch town, ready to enjoy the kingdom's grain and gold.
mahabharata:12:88.9	Whatever concerns the village and the headman, some righteous minister, untiring, should himself oversee.
mahabharata:12:88.11	Considering sale, purchase, road, food, expense, and security and welfare, he should levy taxes on merchants.
mahabharata:12:88.12	Having repeatedly considered the output, the livelihood given and the craft, he should levy on craftsmen corresponding to their craft.
mahabharata:12:88.13	Taxes high and low were just for earlier kings, Yudhishthira; the lord of the earth should act so that they do not decline.
mahabharata:12:88.14	Considering fruit and work, he should arrange all; no one should engage in fruit and work without cause.
mahabharata:12:88.15	As king and doer would both share in the work, the king should always levy taxes after considering.
mahabharata:12:88.16	He should not cut off the root of himself or others out of greed; a king should block the doors of desire, showing kindly affection.
mahabharata:12:88.17	They hate a king who is known as a great devourer; how can one hated find good or the beloved gain the dear?
mahabharata:12:88.18	The kingdom should be milked like a calf by one of untiring wisdom; a supported calf of grown strength bears pain, Bharata.
mahabharata:12:88.19	A calf too much milked does not work, Yudhishthira; a kingdom too much milked also does not do great work.
mahabharata:12:88.20	A king who favours the kingdom and, himself supporting it, lives on what has arisen gains very great fruit.
mahabharata:12:88.21	Kings gather stores here for calamity; the kingdom should be a treasure, and the treasure in the house.
mahabharata:12:88.22	He should show compassion to all townsfolk and country folk, dependants and those close, as far as able, even all the inner ones.
mahabharata:12:88.23	Having divided the outer people, the middle should be enjoyed in comfort; thus people, happy or unhappy, are not enraged.
mahabharata:12:88.24	Before collecting tax, after speaking repeatedly, assembling in his own country, he should show fear in the kingdom:
mahabharata:12:88.25	This calamity has arisen, a great fear from an enemy's army; it might not end, like the bearing of fruit on a bamboo.
My enemies, risen with many robbers, wish to oppress this kingdom for their own destruction.
In this dreadful calamity, a dreadful fear having come, I shall ask your wealth for protection.
And I shall repay you all when the fear is gone; enemies will not repay what they take by force from here.
One's own wealth perishes by itself if one begins with wives; even if wealth is gathered for sons and wives.
I delight in your power as in my sons' and urge you; I favour you as able without oppressing the kingdom.
In calamities you must bear it, like good oxen; I shall not make wealth dearer to you in any calamity."
With such sweet, smooth words and courteous manner he should release his own reins, taking the yoke, knowing the time.
Considering pasturage, the support of servants, expense, the danger from cattle-villages, and security and welfare, he should levy taxes on cattle-owners.
Cattle-owners living in forests perish if neglected; therefore toward them he should act especially gently first.
Conciliation, protection, giving, arrangement, repeated shares and pleasant things should be done for cattle-owners, Partha.
Their produce is to be used constantly; it strengthens the kingdom, trade and agriculture.
Therefore the wise should show affection to cattle-owners with effort, merciful and careful, levying mild taxes.
Security and welfare everywhere are easy for cattle-owners, dear one; there is no wealth like this, Yudhishthira."

According to place, time and strength, a king who seeks dharma and wealth should instruct the subjects, devoted to their welfare.
mahabharata:12:89.3	As he thinks best for them and himself, so the king should set all lawful things in motion in the kingdom.
mahabharata:12:89.4	He should milk the kingdom as honey is milked, not destroying the bees; he should milk looking to the calf and not crush the teats.
mahabharata:12:89.5	He should drink the kingdom like a leech, gently, O king, and take his son like a tigress without biting, that he may not fall.
mahabharata:12:89.6	He should have them give a little at a time, increasing; then more and more, he should bring increase as he likes.
mahabharata:12:89.7	Like taming the tameable, he should always increase the load; with effort and gently he should make them eat from the snares.
mahabharata:12:89.8	Once strewn with snares, they will not be hard to tame; they will be enjoyed, with effort, as is proper.
mahabharata:12:89.9	Therefore a flock of men is hard to manage in everything; conciliating the chief ones, the other people should be enjoyed.
mahabharata:12:89.11	Taxes should not be imposed on them at the wrong place or time, but in order, with conciliation, at the proper time and by rule.
mahabharata:12:89.12	I tell these expedients; no illusion is meant by me; one who tames without means enrages the horses.
mahabharata:12:89.13	Taverns, brothels, brothel-keepers and shopkeepers, entertainers with gamblers, and any others of the kind,
mahabharata:12:89.14	all these who are destroyers of the kingdom are to be restrained; staying in the kingdom, they harass the good people.
mahabharata:12:89.15	No one should ask anyone for anything except in calamity"—this rule for beings was made by Manu long ago.
If all did not live thus and did not work here, the three worlds would surely not be.
A king who is able to restrain and does not restrain them enjoys a fourth of their sin, so the scripture says; and likewise a fourth of the dharma done.
Having come together in these places, in association, the destroyers of prosperity, a man attached to desire, what deed would he avoid?
Those who have no possessions may beg in calamity alone; they should be given by dharma by one wishing mercy, out of compassion.
Let there be no beggars in your kingdom, nor robbers; these are takers of what is offered, not promoters of welfare.
Let those who favour beings and make the subjects flourish be active in your kingdom, not the destroyers of beings.
And those engaged in taking wealth are to be punished, O great king; they should be made to put it to use and pay taxes according to their strength.
Agriculture, cattle-keeping, trade and anything of the kind he should have done by men together with many workers.
If a man engaged in agriculture, cattle-keeping or trade meets with some danger, the king is blamed for it.
He should always honour the wealthy with vehicles, clothing and food, and say to them, "Favour us, honoured with me."
The wealthy are indeed a great limb of kings, Bharata, the hump of all beings; one standing on wealth is without doubt.
The wise, brave, wealthy lord who is righteous, an ascetic, truthful and intelligent protects.
Therefore be affectionate to all of these, lord of the earth, and maintain truth, uprightness, freedom from anger and kindness.
Thus you will gain rod, treasury, friends and land, devoted to truth and uprightness, O king, with friends and treasury."

Let others eat what is left over by Brahmanas; none else should take in any way by obstructing a Brahmana.
mahabharata:12:90.3	If a Brahmana should take to renunciation, wasted by lack of livelihood, a livelihood should be provided for him, lord of men, with his wife.
mahabharata:12:90.4	If he does not turn back, it should be said in the assembly of Brahmanas: 'In what will this world now make a boundary?'
mahabharata:12:90.5	He would surely turn back if he does not speak after this; this rule should first be indirectly made, Kaunteya.
mahabharata:12:90.6	People say this, Brahmana, but I do not believe it; he should be invited with enjoyments; if he has no livelihood, then let him act.
mahabharata:12:90.7	Agriculture, cattle-keeping and trade are the livelihood of people here, and above them the triple learning; it makes beings flourish.
mahabharata:12:90.8	When it strives, those who obstruct it are robbers; for their slaying here Brahma created the kshatriya order.
mahabharata:12:90.9	Slay your enemies, protect the subjects, sacrifice with sacrifices, O king, and fight in battle as a hero, delight of the Kurus.
mahabharata:12:90.14	What is the weak point, what is my attachment, what remains unfelled? From where might fault flow to me?"—he should think thus always.
By approved secret spies he should have the earth surveyed: "Do they praise my conduct as well conducted or not? Does my fame please in the country, in the kingdom?
Those who know dharma and are steadfast, who do not flee in battles, and those who live in the kingdom and those who live on the king,
and all ministers and all those who are neutral, those who praise you or revile you—all of them, Yudhishthira, should be well led.
It is not possible, dear one, to please everyone entirely—friend, enemy or neutral—among all beings, Bharata.
Among those of equal strength of arm who are devoted to qualities, how could one be superior and enjoy men?
The moving eat the unmoving, the tuskless the tusked, as enraged venomous snakes eat snakes.
Be ever careful of these, Yudhishthira; for these, like bharunda birds, fall on one who is careless.
Are your merchants in your kingdom not troubled, oppressed by taxes, buying much for little and labouring in wild places?
Do the farmers, much oppressed, not leave the kingdom, they who bear the king's burden and support others as well?
Gods and hosts of ancestors live on what is given from here, as do men, serpents, Rakshasas, birds and animals.
This is your livelihood of the kingdom and protection of the kingdom, Bharata; relying on this very aim I shall speak more, Pandava."

How Utathya, the best knower of Brahma, instructed him—all that I shall tell you in full, Yudhishthira.
mahabharata:12:91.3	A king exists for dharma, not for acting at will; know thus, Mandhata, that a king is the protector of the world.
A king who practises dharma goes to godhood; if he does not practise dharma he goes to hell.
Beings stand in dharma and dharma stands in the king; a king who rules well is lord of the earth.
A king supremely righteous but fortunate is called sinful; the gods are rebuked and it is said, "There is no dharma."
Success of aims is seen for those who act unrighteously; and the world follows all that as auspicious.
The conduct of dharma is uprooted and great unrighteousness prevails; they call it fear day and night when sin is not restrained.
The twice-born who keep vows do not follow the Vedas, Brahmanas do not extend sacrifices, when sin is not restrained.
In whom dharma shines, they call him king; in whom dharma is dissolved, the gods know him as a vrishala (outcast).
Dharma, the revered one, is the bull (vrisha); one who sufficiently harms it, the gods know as a vrishala; therefore one should not destroy dharma.
When dharma grows all beings grow; when it declines they decline; therefore one should increase dharma.
Dharma flows from wealth, or is certain from upholding; lord of men, it is called the one that ends the boundary of what should not be done.
For the prosperity of beings dharma was created by the Self-existent himself; therefore one should increase dharma for the favour of subjects.
Therefore, tiger among kings, dharma is held best; that is the king who rules the subjects well, best of men.
Disregarding desire and anger, one should protect dharma alone; dharma is the most beneficial for kings, best of the Bharatas.
Brahmanas are the source of dharma; therefore always honour them, and fulfil the wishes of Brahmanas without envy, Mandhata.
By not fulfilling their wishes fear arises for the king, friends do not prosper and even become enemies.
When Bali, son of Virochana, was envious of Brahmanas, then Shri, who was in him, resplendent, left him.
Departing from him, she went to Pakashasana; then he repented afterward seeing Shri in Purandara.
This is the fruit of envy and pride, overcomer; therefore understand, Mandhata, lest the resplendent one leave you.
Pride, named Darpa, a son of Shri, was born of adharma, the scripture says; by him gods and asuras, O king, were brought under sway very often.
And many royal sages too; therefore understand, lord of the earth: a king who conquers him becomes king, and he who is conquered by him is a slave.
So act, Mandhata, as to not serve unrighteousness accompanied by pride, if you wish to stay long.
One should beware of the drunk, the careless, the adolescent, and especially the mad; from practice of that, from association, from serving the unfriendly,
from a restrained minister, and especially from women, from mountains, uneven ground, forts, elephants, horses and reptiles.
Of these one should always be careful, and avoid night-wandering; one should avoid excess in income, excess in pride, hypocrisy and anger.
A king should not have intercourse with unknown women, eunuchs, unchaste women, others' wives or maidens.
In families Rakshasa-like sinners are born through mixture of classes, deformed, limb-lacking, thick-tongued, senseless.
These and others are born when the king is careless; therefore a king should act especially for the welfare of the people.
A great fault arises in a careless kshatriya; unrighteous things proceed, causing mixture of the subjects.
Cold is found in the not cold, and no cold in the cold; drought and excessive rain and disease enter the subjects.
Stars stand ominous and other dreadful planets, and many portents destructive of kings are seen here.
A king who does not guard himself and does not guard his subjects has his subjects waste away, and he perishes after them.
Two take from one, and many from two; maidens are ruined; this they call the king's fault.
The idea "this is mine" does not stay among men when the king abandons dharma and practises carelessness."

As a washerman who does not know how to remove the dirt from garments or cleanse coloured ones is as if he did not exist,
mahabharata:12:92.3	so it is with the best of the twice-born, kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras; the four classes abide in their various works.
By the deed this one did, he met death; the cause of his destruction is his deed; we are all under the sway of deeds.
Svaninetra, valiant, having won an unthorned kingdom, could not protect it, and the subjects were not attached to him.
At every step the revered Vyasa, the great-souled Sanjaya and Gandhari—this very thing torments me today.
Then Kritavarman, greatly enraged, said to him, pointing as if scornfully with his left hand:
My brothers have fallen here; let them come with me; without my brothers I do not wish to go to heaven, lord of the gods.
What stain of deed was done by these great souls, by Karna, by the sons of Draupadi, or by the slender-waisted Panchali?
